title: Detection of Exploits
summary: This strategy detects Exploits, the resource development step in which an adversary obtains exploit code or a turnkey exploit tool for a vulnerability they intend to use. It matters because acquiring a weapon is one of the last preparations before an intrusion attempt, so the signal is close in time to real risk. Detection relies on web proxy and DNS logs for requests to exploit repositories, endpoint file creation events for archive and script downloads into temporary paths, and process creation showing a recently downloaded file executed moments later. The common failure mode is that much exploit traffic happens off corporate networks, so visibility is strongest for internal downloads, penetration testing activity, and repository access from developer hosts.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for signs that someone is downloading or collecting exploit code. An exploit is a piece of software that abuses a flaw in a program. The detection watches file downloads, web requests, and the moment a downloaded file is run.
beginner.whyItMatters: Exploit code is a weapon, and collecting it shows clear intent to attack. The download often happens shortly before the first real attempt. Your own security team also downloads these files for testing. That creates noise, but it also means the pattern is well understood. With good context you can tell approved testing from an unknown actor quietly gathering tools.
howItWorks: A proxy or firewall records each web request, including the site name and the user agent text.
The endpoint agent records each new file and the command line of each new process.
The rule flags requests and downloads linked to known exploit hosting or exploit keywords.
It then looks for a process that runs a file written to a temporary folder minutes earlier.
Records are joined by host, user, and time so that unrelated events do not match.
Filtered sources, such as the approved penetration testing range, are removed before alerting.
beginner.example: Imagine a shop that sells both kitchen knives and tools for burglars. Buying a knife is normal and tells you little. Buying a lock pick set at two in the morning, then walking to a locked building, tells a story. The detection does not care about one download by itself. It cares when the download and the very next action point the same way, from a source you do not recognise.
takeaways: Exploit collection is one of the last steps before an attack, so it deserves attention.
A download alone is weak evidence; the download followed by immediate execution is much stronger.
Approved testing and research activity must be separated by source, not by file name.

objectives: Describe what exploit code is and why obtaining it is a detectable preparation step
Name the telemetry that records web requests, file creation, and process start events
Correlate a file download with the process that executes it shortly afterwards
Design filters that separate approved penetration testing from unknown collection activity
Decide an appropriate severity for exploit acquisition relative to later intrusion stages
dataSources: Web proxy request logs with full URL, user agent, and authenticated user identity
Sysmon event 1 process creation including parent image and full command line
Sysmon event 11 file creation events for archives and scripts written to temporary directories
DNS resolver query logs for exploit hosting and paste style domains
Endpoint detection and response file download telemetry with file hash and signing status
logic: The pattern is the acquisition and first use of exploit material on a managed host: a web or DNS request that resolves to an exploit repository or an archive download into a temporary path, followed within minutes by a process that executes from that same path. The fields that must be correlated are the host name, the user account, the destination domain, the written file path, and the command line of the child process. Benign activity comes from vulnerability management staff and penetration testers who download the same content from known network ranges on planned days. The malicious case is an unapproved host or user, often arriving through a browser with an unusual user agent, where the download and the execution pair tightly and the file is unsigned.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Exploit Download Followed By Execution
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   category: proxy
# detection:
#   selection:
#     Url|contains:
#       - 'exploit-db'
#       - 'poc'
#       - 'cve-'
#     FileExtension|contains:
#       - '.zip'
#       - '.rar'
#       - '.py'
#   filter:
#     SourceIp|cidr: '10[.]20[.]0[.]0/16'
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: high
falsePositives: Penetration testers downloading proof of concept code from an approved testing workstation range
Security researchers and vulnerability analysts collecting code samples for triage in a lab network
Developers cloning public repositories that contain exploit proof of concept files for patch validation
Training platforms and capture the flag events where participants download vulnerable applications
tuningNotes: Baseline which hosts and users touch exploit related content, then allowlist by authenticated user and source range rather than by URL keyword, because the keyword list ages quickly. Enrich with external threat intelligence and internet facing destination reputation, and require the execution step before raising severity to high. Scope the alert to user workstations and jump hosts, and keep a hunt only version on developer and research networks. The trade off is that narrowing to execution pairs will miss an adversary who stages the file for later use, and dropping keyword matching will lose early warning of collection activity.
